title: AES-128 K9 four-byte tail: chosen bytes (Giraud, AES2004 proceedings published 2005)

target.description: Full AES-128; recover only K9[12..15], a 32-bit group of the penultimate round key.

setting.key_relation: One fixed secret AES master key; no related-key oracle.
setting.key_population: Keys of the stated AES implementation without a weak-key restriction; fault protections are outside the model.
setting.plaintext_model: Repeat encryptions of the same plaintext under the same key; retain its correct ciphertext as a reference. Counts of faulty ciphertexts exclude that reusable reference unless explicitly stated otherwise.

fault_model.target: A byte of K9 after its correct use in round 9, before online derivation of K10.
fault_model.granularity: One initially affected byte, followed by propagation through the key schedule or AES rounds.
fault_model.timing: After the correct round-9 key addition and before generating K10.
fault_model.location: Choose each of K9[12..15] in turn, with repeated faults on that byte.
fault_model.value_control: The byte difference is unknown; its value may be inferred or guessed from correct/faulty outputs.
fault_model.sample_pairing: Every faulty output is matched to the same fixed-input correct reference; useful faults, random-location ciphertexts and physical executions have distinct accounting.

assumptions: A round key is used correctly for encryption and then faulted before generating the next round key. The implementation expands keys on the fly.
The reported outcome and data budget use the paper's candidate-filtering model; no numerical whole-key success rate is inferred from a byte-level statistic.

time.note: No numerical whole-endpoint runtime is reported for this version and endpoint.

data.note: Two suitable distinct fault values for each of four chosen K9 bytes; the source supplies no numeric joint success.

memory.note: The article describes counters or candidate lists without a numerical peak-memory budget.

preprocessing.note: No separate reusable preprocessing-time budget is reported. The Appendix A 8×2^8 equation tests per useful output are a component count, not a complete attack cost.

success.description: No numerical whole-output recovery probability is supplied for this exact endpoint and sample budget. The K9 two-distinct-byte-fault uniqueness assertion has an existing counterexample; the32-fault tail and240-fault cumulative quantities are acquisition/mean counts, not success probabilities. Existing source conflicts remain unresolved. No byte-level90%/99% rate or product of marginal probabilities is assigned as whole-output success.

review.scope: Exact15-page proceedings edition; Sections4–6 and AppendixA. No probability was added: byte-equation candidate retention, special-byte90%/99% and mean fault counts do not quantify these cumulative or complete outputs. Software250-fault demonstration has no repeated-trial rate. Existing two-fault uniqueness and M8/M9 timing conflicts remain unchanged; not a new full-paper audit.

components.description: Sections4.1–4.3: with effective faults at the modeled windows and correct earlier-stage material, the actual subkey/state satisfies the complete candidate equations. This is conditional candidate inclusion, not unique recovery or physical acquisition success.

field_conflicts.label: Two distinct byte faults do not guarantee uniqueness
field_conflicts.description: Section4.1 asserts that two different nonzero byte differences leave only the trueK9byte. Independent exact AES enumeration gives x=00,e=01,e′=bc: both Eq15 candidate sets are{00,01,bc,bd}. Master key7397d3478f25232538f49e9f10989845 realizes all-zeroK9. Two observations are not an unconditional uniqueness certificate. Downstream sample counts remain source claims; no replacement cost, success or attack-impossibility conclusion is inferred.
